In ring-closing metathesis (RCM) of a 1,7-octadiene, the two terminal alkene carbons (C-1 and C-8) each lose a CH₂ fragment as ethene, and the two internal vinylic carbons (C-2 and C-7) form the new C=C bond of the ring.  
Thus the six-membered ring that results is composed of carbons 2-3-4-5-6-7 of the starting octadiene:

 C₂ (→ ring C-1) = C₇ (→ ring C-2) – C₆ (→ ring C-3) – C₅ (→ ring C-4) – C₄ (→ ring C-5) – C₃ (→ ring C-6)

Therefore, any substituent originally on:

• C₃ becomes substituent on ring C-6 (or C-3, depending on numbering)  
• C₄ becomes substituent on ring C-5 (or C-4)  
• C₅ becomes substituent on ring C-4 (or C-5)

To obtain 5-isopropyl-3,4-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene we need:

• methyl groups on the carbons that will become ring C-3 and C-4 → these are C₃ and C₄ of the open chain  
• an isopropyl group on the carbon that will become ring C-5 → this is C₅ of the open chain  
• terminal double bonds at C-1 and C-8 (a 1,7-diene) to give a six-membered ring.

Among the options, compound (A) 5-isopropyl-3,4-dimethylocta-1,7-diene has:

C-1 = CH₂=  C-2 = CH–  C-3 = CH(CH₃)–  C-4 = CH(CH₃)–  C-5 = C(isopropyl)H–  C-6-C-7-C-8=CH₂

Thus after RCM (bonding C-2 to C-7) it furnishes exactly 5-isopropyl-3,4-dimethylcyclohex-1-ene.

The other dienes either have the double bonds at the wrong positions (2,6-diene or 1,6-diene) or place the substituents on the wrong carbons.

Hence the correct starting material is:

(A) 5-isopropyl-3,4-dimethylocta-1,7-diene

Answer: A
